quotes: “Given the above, tribunals should be cautious about proceeding with a twin-track approach to a case without good cause. A party may be advocating bifurcation to delay and obstruct the arbitration, rather than to make it more efficient.”
“A tribunal should be suspicious of a party's motives in advocating bifurcation and alert to whether identifying a preliminary issue results in a genuine saving of time or not.”

“Presently, bifurcation is a blunt tool which can be effective (in terms of shortening the duration of a case) only in certain circumstances [...]. Essentially, arbitrators are largely rolling the dice as to whether the bifurcated issue is one that will dispose of the proceedings.”

“[...] the data suggests there should be a presumption against agreeing to bifurcate proceedings (on efficiency grounds) unless a tribunal can be confident that it is more likely than not that determination of the bifurcated issue [...] will result in termination of the proceeding.”

“Of course, at times requests to be heard may reflect abusive strategies consisting in 'guerrilla tactics'. [...] It is the true intention of the party that matters in discerning whether a certain request is made in good faith.”
“In practice, the choice for bifurcation is based on speculative assumptions. Consequently, it seems essential to provide a tool to assess when bifurcation is appropriate.”

“Since challenges are sometimes used for purely tactical reasons, it is good practice for arbitrators to confirm with the parties that they do not have objections to the arbitrators' jurisdiction to decide the matter.”

“Considerations to be taken into account include the likely success of the challenge and whether they consider that it was made in good faith or just as a device to disrupt and/or delay the arbitration.”

“Conversely, if the challenge is closely related to the substantive issues of the dispute, or where the arbitrators consider it to be a mere tactical device to delay the proceedings, arbitrators should continue with the proceedings and incorporate their decision on jurisdiction into the final award on the merits.”

“Professionals involved in the arbitration may have an opposite interest to prolong the proceedings if their remuneration is based on the time spent, while parties may use bifurcation as a mere dilatory tactic: of course, these are not interests worth of protection.”

“Indeed, if bifurcation has been devised for the purpose of addressing a defence which could dispose of the entire dispute and the defence is rejected by the arbitral tribunal, then bifurcation will produce the opposite result of increasing the time and costs of the proceedings.”

“Another potential counterargument against the implementation of a system of dynamic bifurcation is that it might be used as a weapon to stall or derail the proceedings. The worry here is that simply raising a 'frivolous' jurisdictional defence would be sufficient to have (the majority of) the arbitral tribunal replaced [...]”

“In this sense, Tribunals need to be extremely careful when applying both Bifurcation and Reconsideration: if they are to apply too lenient standards this can lead to inefficient proceedings (1) unnecessarily separating a proceeding into phases not needed to render a decision multiplying party submissions and Tribunal decisions, thereby increasing the time and expense of the proceedings...”
